name: Lachlan Giles and Ariel Tabak Guard Retention System
description: Study guard retention against around-the-legs and stacking passes with a practical BJJGraph guide to Lachlan Giles and Ariel Tabak's BJJ Fanatics course.
summary: The Lachlan Giles and Ariel Tabak Guard Retention System is a BJJGraph study guide for recovering useful frames and leg position against around-the-legs and under-the-legs passes.
overview:
A passer who clears your feet may still have to get past your knees, elbows, and ability to turn toward them. This guide organizes practice around recognizing which defensive layer remains available and rebuilding contact before trying to attack. It is most useful when you can already identify open guard, side control, and the difference between retaining guard and escaping a settled pin.

The optional course companion is The Guard Retention Anthology: Around and Under by Lachlan Giles and Ariel Tabak. Its published syllabus addresses general retention concepts, movement, around-the-legs passing, under-the-legs passing, and specific passing situations. This page is an independent BJJGraph practice plan, not the instructors' official curriculum. Adapt the movement choices to your mobility and use a coach to check any unfamiliar inversion or stacking situation.
key_principles: Identify the passer's route before choosing a recovery movement.
Keep usable frames between the passer and your torso.
Recover leg position before committing to an attack.
Move enough to restore a barrier rather than moving continuously without a purpose.
Separate early guard retention from escaping a settled pin.
Choose movements that remain controlled within your available mobility.

key_components.description: Distinguish a passer circling the legs from one lifting or folding them toward the torso.
key_components.purpose: Choose a relevant defensive task instead of rehearsing an unrelated response.

key_components.description: Use the arms to maintain workable space while the legs are temporarily displaced by the passer.
key_components.purpose: Preserve enough room to rebuild a leg barrier.

key_components.description: Return a foot, shin, or knee to useful contact as the passer changes direction and distance.
key_components.purpose: Rebuild a playable guard rather than merely delay the pass.

key_components.description: Explore a small set of recovery movements with your coach and select those you can perform without forcing range.
key_components.purpose: Keep the practice applicable to your body and current skill.

key_components.description: After recovering contact, establish a guard you can use and observe the passer's next response.
key_components.purpose: Connect defense to a stable next decision.

implementation_sequence.description: Start in open guard with the passer outside the legs and agree on one passing route.
Pause when the feet are displaced and locate the next frame or leg connection you can preserve.
key_points: Notice where the passer's weight is.
Avoid reaching without a specific purpose.

implementation_sequence.description: Use a controlled recovery movement to bring a leg back between your torso and the passer.
key_points: Ask your coach to check unfamiliar mechanics.

implementation_sequence.description: Establish usable contact before treating the repetition as finished.
key_points: Check whether the passer can immediately clear the same barrier.

implementation_sequence.description: Let the passer change direction once so you must recognize and solve a second problem.
key_points: Keep resistance low enough to observe the transition.

implementation_sequence.description: Use short rounds with defined passing options and compare the results with your practice notes.
key_points: Separate a retention failure from a pin escape.
Select one recurring issue for the next session.

common_obstacles.obstacle: Moving the legs without restoring contact
common_obstacles.solution: Define the specific foot, shin, or knee barrier you intend to recover before repeating the movement.

common_obstacles.obstacle: Using the same response against every passing route
common_obstacles.solution: Constrain the passer to one route first, then contrast it with a second route and describe the changed problem.

common_obstacles.obstacle: Treating flexibility as a substitute for positioning
common_obstacles.solution: Reduce the range and speed, select another movement when necessary, and have a coach check alignment.

common_obstacles.obstacle: Starting offense before guard is stable
common_obstacles.solution: Add a brief stabilization task after recovery so the passer can test whether the contact is useful.

common_obstacles.obstacle: Practicing too many recoveries at once
common_obstacles.solution: Keep one recurring passing problem in focus and record the cue that makes your chosen response relevant.

assessment_metrics.description: Identify how the passer is getting beyond your legs.
proficiency_indicators: Notice a direction change before the torso is pinned.
Explain what changed between successive attempts.

assessment_metrics.description: Observe whether usable space survives the recovery attempt.
proficiency_indicators: Keep a frame available while the legs move.
Recognize when the passer has removed that frame.
Avoid continuing a movement after its space has disappeared.

assessment_metrics.description: Assess the guard you actually reach.
proficiency_indicators: Face the passer in a usable position.
Hold the recovered configuration against a modest follow-up.

assessment_metrics.description: Evaluate whether practice remains repeatable and informative.
proficiency_indicators: Reduce intensity when movement becomes forced.
Record one specific adjustment for the next session.

training_methodology.drilling_approach: Use short partner drills with a clearly defined pass and recovery destination. Begin with a cooperative passer, pause at the point where the first barrier is lost, and identify the remaining options. Add resistance only when the movement stays controlled. Keep late stacking and unfamiliar inversions separate from free sparring until a coach has checked the mechanics. The stages below are BJJGraph practice suggestions.

progression_path.focus: Identify around-the-legs and under-the-legs pressure from cooperative starts.
Practice one comfortable frame-and-leg recovery against a predictable pass.
Allow one direction change and keep track of which barrier you are rebuilding.
Use limited positional rounds to find recurring failures and return to focused drilling.

common_mistakes: Collecting movements without understanding the passing problem.
Calling a brief delay a successful guard recovery.
Forcing unfamiliar ranges under stacking pressure.
Skipping the transition from recovery to a usable guard.

flashcards.question: What should you identify before selecting a guard-retention response?
flashcards.answer: Identify the passer's route and which defensive barriers remain available; the same movement will not solve every passing situation.
flashcards.answer_line: Read the route and remaining barriers

flashcards.question: Why does clearing the feet not always mean the guard has been passed?
flashcards.answer: The knees, elbows, and remaining frames may still prevent the passer from controlling the torso and allow useful leg contact to be restored.
flashcards.answer_line: Other barriers can still protect the torso

flashcards.question: When is a retention repetition complete?
flashcards.answer: Finish after recovering a usable guard that can withstand an agreed follow-up, rather than stopping at a momentary delay in the pass.
flashcards.answer_line: Recover and stabilize a usable guard

flashcards.question: How should you choose a recovery movement for your current mobility?
flashcards.answer: Choose a movement you can perform with control in the required range and ask a coach to check unfamiliar mechanics before adding pressure.

flashcards.question: How can a partner drill reveal a recurring retention mistake?
flashcards.answer: Limit the passer to one route, pause when contact is lost, and record the barrier you failed to preserve before testing one adjustment.
flashcards.answer_line: Constrain the pass and inspect lost contact

flashcards.question: What changes once the passer establishes a settled pin?
flashcards.answer: The immediate task becomes escaping the pin; reset a retention drill or switch deliberately to an escape drill instead of treating them as identical.
flashcards.answer_line: A settled pin calls for an escape

products.title: The Guard Retention Anthology: Around and Under
products.blurb: A dedicated retention course whose published outline includes around-the-legs and under-the-legs passing situations.
products.best_for: Guard players studying those passing routes. Close-range and through-the-legs defense is addressed in a separate companion course.
products.study_focus: Start with the general concepts and movement sections, then choose the around-the-legs or under-the-legs section that matches a recurring passing problem.
products.practice_tip: BJJGraph drill: limit the passer to one route and pause when the first barrier is cleared. Identify the remaining frame before trying to recover a playable guard.
